newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK set for gala of century, but guests uncertain.
newsitem.headline: HK set for gala of century, but guests uncertain.

text.p: Hong Kong unveiled plans on Monday for its ceremony of the century, but with four weeks to go until the handover to China there were holes in the guest list and controversy over how the future government will be sworn in.

The opportunity to witness the end of 156 years of British colonial rule and resumption of Chinese control over the territory of 6.4 million people on July 1 is becoming a magnet for thousands of tourists, hundreds of foreign dignitaries and an army of journalists.

Dozens of celebrations and parades are planned to mark the handover, but it is the official events -- culminating with the lowering of the British Union Jack and raising of the China's red, five-starred flag at midnight on June 30 -- that most symbolise the changes taking place in Hong Kong.

More than 4,000 guests, invited by Britain and China, are expected to attend a gala banquet and witness the official handover ceremony in the Grand Hall of a HK$4.8 billion (US$620 million) extension to the Hong Kong Convention Centre.
They will include ministers from more than 40 countries and 40 international organisations, Stephen Lam, director of the handover ceremony coordination office, told reporters.

U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and former British prime minister Margaret Thatcher would attend, he said, although there were "still several hundred nominations expected" to be put forward by London and Beijing.
The British side is anchored by Prince Charles, Foreign Secretary Robin Cook and Governor Chris Patten.
"The Chinese said have said they will match this," Lam said.
Lam would not say which Chinese official would be the protocol equivalent of the Prince of Wales, but added he was confident Beijing would send a senior leader.
Despite media reports, there has been no confirmation that Chinese President Jiang Zemin will attend and doubts linger about Prime Minister Tony Blair making the trip from London.
"No decision has been made on whether the Prime Minister will visit for the handover ceremony," Lam said.

Britain's Sunday Times newspaper said at the weekend Blair may boycott the ceremony over concerns China planned to use the event to swear in the unelected provisional legislature that will replace the current Legislative Council, relying on the room full of dignitaries to imply international support.
But the office of post-handover leader Tung Chee-hwa said on Monday the inauguration ceremony would be held an hour and a half into Chinese rule in another hall of the Convention Centre.
China's State Council would invite about 4,400 international and local dignitaries to witness the swearing in of Tung, the provisonal legislature and top judges, it said in a statement.
Lam said it was up to guests at the handover ceremony to decide whether they would attend the inauguration. "How many ceremonies they prefer to attend is their business," he said.
With Britain as host, Lam said food at the banquet will be Western -- "a relatively straight-forward, three-course meal".

The programme for the 30- to 45-minute handover ceremony had been agreed. But with Sino-British relations and international protocol to consider, the seating plan was "very difficult" to arrange, he said.
Prince Charles will speak at the official ceremony before he and Patten board the royal yacht Britannia just after midnight to sail away from what is now Britain's last major colony.
To mark the first day of Chinese rule on July 1, Hong Kong's business community is planning an extravaganza of fireworks, lasers and a flotilla of illuminated barges.
But the territory's democracy movement said on Monday it would stage its own parade on July 1 -- a protest march to test Beijing's pledge that free expression will survive the handover.
